135.title: John the Baptist
135.b0.ask: “How did John — the last of the old prophets and the herald of a new age — prepare the way, and then gladly decrease?”
135.b2.p: In Paper 134 Jesus heard that John had reached the neighborhood of Pella, laid down his tools, and said, “⟦Q 135:8.3|135:8.5|134:9.8⟧My hour has come.⟦/Q⟧” Paper 135 goes back in time and tells, from the beginning, who that John was. He was born on March 25, 7 B.C., in keeping with Gabriel’s promise to Elizabeth. Yet apart from Gabriel’s visit and the dream of Zacharias, there was nothing unusual or supernatural about his birth.
135.b3.p: John grew up as an ordinary child in a small village west of Jerusalem. The great event of his early childhood was a visit, at about six years of age, to Jesus and the family at Nazareth. His father Zacharias was a priest, his mother Elizabeth was far better educated than most women of Judea, and since John was their only child, they gave much time to his mental and spiritual training.
135.b4.p: How did this young shepherd of the wilderness become the preacher who stirred all Palestine — and what did he hold on to through the long waiting of his imprisonment?
135.b5.q: ⟦Q 135:11.2⟧He must increase but I must decrease.⟦/Q⟧
135.b8.p: When John was fourteen, his parents took him to Engedi by the Dead Sea, the southern headquarters of the Nazarite brotherhood, and there he was solemnly inducted into the order for life. He took the same life vows as Samson and the prophet Samuel. Life Nazarites were the only persons besides the high priest ever permitted to enter the holy of holies, and the Jews regarded them with almost the same respect.
135.b9.t: Refrain from touching the dead, even in one’s own family
135.b10.p: At sixteen John read about Elijah and was so impressed that from that day on he always wore a hairy garment with a leather girdle. Already more than six feet tall, with his flowing hair and peculiar dress, he was indeed a picturesque youth.
135.b12.p: In A.D. 12, when John was eighteen, his father died. Because the Nazarite vow forbade contact with the dead, even one’s own family, John was deeply troubled, and after the burial he went to Jerusalem to offer the sacrifices for his cleansing. That September he visited Nazareth, ready to launch out on his lifework. But Jesus’ words and example persuaded him to go home, take care of his mother, and await “⟦Q 135:2.2⟧the coming of the Father’s hour.⟦/Q⟧” The two did not meet again until the baptism in the Jordan.
135.b13.p: Because John refused the priest’s allowance due him from the temple funds, the family nearly lost its home, and mother and son moved south to Hebron. John tended sheep in the wilderness of Judea and often visited the Nazarite brotherhood at Engedi. He was so different from most of the Nazarites that he found it hard to fit in, but he was very fond of Abner, the head of the colony.
135.b15.p: Along a little brook John built more than a dozen stone shelters and night corrals. With Ezda, an orphan boy he had in a way adopted, he lived very simply on mutton, goat’s milk, wild honey, and locusts. The shepherd’s life gave him plenty of time to think. He loved the writings of the prophet Daniel and read a thousand times Daniel’s description of the great image that stood for the great kingdoms of the world.
135.b16.t: Made of so many peoples it could never be firmly consolidated
The kingdom of the God of heaven
A kingdom which shall never be destroyed
135.b17.p: John never quite reconciled what his parents had told him about Jesus with Daniel’s words about “⟦Q 135:3.3⟧one like the Son of Man.⟦/Q⟧” Still, his mother assured him that his distant cousin Jesus was the true Messiah and that John was to be his herald. Hearing of the wickedness of Rome and the evil doings of Herod, John came to believe that the end of the age was near, and the feeling grew in his heart that he was to be the last of the old prophets and the first of the new.
135.b19.p: In A.D. 22, when John was twenty-eight, his mother died suddenly. After the funeral he gave his flocks to the brotherhood and withdrew for a season to fast and pray. He knew only the old ways of approaching God — the ways of Elijah, Samuel, and Daniel. For two and a half years he lived at Engedi, reading over and over the last five chapters of Isaiah and the prophet Malachi.
135.b20.p: Malachi’s promise that Elijah would come before the day of the Lord held John back for more than two years. He knew he was not Elijah, and he never called himself by that name. Yet Elijah’s influence led him to attack the sins of his day directly and bluntly. He was a clear thinker, a powerful speaker, and a fiery denunciator. At last, in March of A.D. 25, he swept aside all doubts and left Engedi to begin his public preaching.
135.b22.p: To understand John’s message we must know the condition of the Jewish people. For almost a hundred years Israel had been unable to explain why God’s chosen people remained subject to gentile rulers. A new school of teachers, the apocalyptists, taught that the Jews were paying the penalty for the nation’s sins and that this discipline was nearly over. To the Jews of Palestine, the “⟦Q 135:3.2|135:3.4|135:4.3⟧kingdom of heaven⟦/Q⟧” meant an absolutely righteous state in which God would rule the nations of earth as he rules in heaven.
135.b23.t: A regenerated Jewish nation ruled by David’s successor
Not of this world — a new heaven and a new earth
A world-wide war that destroys all unbelievers
The great judgment of God on the unrighteous
Many devout gentiles might be admitted
135.b24.p: There was disagreement, too, about who the Messiah would be. The older teachers clung to the son of David; the newer ones looked for “⟦Q 135:3.3|135:5.5|135:5.7⟧the Son of Man,⟦/Q⟧” a heavenly Prince long held in waiting at God’s right hand. So John’s announcement of the coming kingdom had at least half a dozen different meanings for his hearers — yet every group was drawn to his preaching.
135.b26.p: Early in March of A.D. 25 John began to preach at the Bethany ford, where Joshua had led Israel into the promised land. He came from the herdsmen like Amos, dressed like Elijah, and thundered his warnings in the “⟦Q 135:6.3⟧spirit and power of Elijah.⟦/Q⟧” He baptized his believers “⟦Q 135:6.4|136:2.1⟧for the remission of sins.⟦/Q⟧” Gentile converts had long been baptized, but never before had the Jews themselves been asked to submit to the baptism of repentance. In the fifteen months before his arrest he baptized well over one hundred thousand penitents.
135.b27.p: John was a heroic but tactless preacher. When Pharisees and Sadducees came for baptism, he warned them not to say that Abraham was their father, but to bring forth fruit worthy of sincere repentance. He also taught his disciples what the new life should look like in practice.
135.b28.t: Teach the spirit as well as the letter of the law
Extort no more than that which is assigned you
Do no violence and be content with your wages
Make ready for the end of the age — the kingdom of heaven is at hand
135.b30.p: John still had confused ideas about the coming kingdom and its king. The longer he preached, the more confused he became, yet his conviction that the kingdom was about to appear never weakened in the least. In mind John might be confused, but in spirit never.
135.b31.p: Traveling north up the Jordan, at Adam his disciples asked him outright whether he was the Messiah. For the first time he spoke of another who was to come after him, one so much greater that he was not worthy to unloose his sandal straps: “⟦Q 135:7.2⟧I baptize you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.⟦/Q⟧” Day by day his teaching grew more helpful and comforting.
135.b33.p: At noon on Sunday, January 13, A.D. 26, Jesus laid down his tools in the boatshop and announced, “⟦Q 135:8.3|135:8.5|134:9.8⟧My hour has come.⟦/Q⟧” With his brothers James and Jude he set out for Pella, and there they took their places in the line of penitents waiting for baptism. When John recognized him, he said that he needed to be baptized by Jesus instead. Jesus whispered that they should set this example for his brothers, so that the people might know his hour had come.
135.b34.p: At noon on Monday, January 14, John baptized Jesus and his two brothers. As the people were leaving, the four men still standing in the water saw an apparition appear for a moment over Jesus’ head and heard a voice. Jesus came up out of the water in silence and went toward the hills to the east, and no one saw him again for forty days.
135.b35.q: ⟦Q 135:8.6|135:9.7|136:2.3⟧This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased.⟦/Q⟧
135.b37.p: During the forty days Jesus was away, John’s preaching took on new and certain notes of proclamation. About three weeks later a deputation of priests and Pharisees came from Jerusalem to question him.
135.b38.t: Are you the prophet Moses promised?
There has been among us one who will return to baptize you with the Holy Spirit
135.b39.p: Among his disciples a debate arose: would the Messiah be a military leader who would strike Rome, or one who had come to set up a spiritual kingdom? John leaned, with the minority, toward the spiritual kingdom, though he was not clear about what it would include. When some wanted to go in search of Jesus, he forbade it, saying that their times were in the hands of the God of heaven. On the morning of February 23 Jesus returned, and John stood on a large rock and cried, “⟦Q 135:9.7⟧Behold the Son of God, the deliverer of the world!⟦/Q⟧” The next morning the two parted on the banks of the Jordan, never again to meet in the flesh.
135.b41.p: After Jesus went north to Galilee, John turned south. About a quarter of his followers had already gone to Galilee to find Jesus. John felt that the responsibility for the coming kingdom was no longer on his shoulders and that his work was nearly done. He was disconsolate and lonely, but he kept preaching and baptizing. His message gradually became a proclamation of mercy for the common people, while he denounced the corrupt rulers more fiercely than ever.
135.b42.p: Near Adam he publicly attacked Herod Antipas for unlawfully taking another man’s wife. Herod, fearing a rebellion and resenting the criticism, had John arrested early on the morning of June 12, A.D. 26. His disciples scattered, and many went to Galilee to join the followers of Jesus.
135.b44.p: For more than a year and a half this rugged man of God’s outdoors languished in prison. He was often tempted to doubt: if Jesus were the Messiah, why did he do nothing to set him free? When his disciples complained that Jesus prospered while doing nothing for him, John answered that he was the friend of the bridegroom, who rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. He realized that he had spoken a prophecy, and never again did he wholly doubt Jesus’ mission and divinity.
135.b45.p: Jesus loved John greatly, but knowing that John’s work on earth was finished and that great things awaited him beyond, he did not interfere with the natural course of his career. A few days before his death John sent once more to ask whether Jesus was truly the Messiah. Jesus sent word that he had not forgotten him, that John should bear this too, and that the poor were having good tidings preached to them. This last message greatly comforted John and steadied his faith.
135.b47.p: John was held in the fortress of Machaerus. Herod was afraid to release him lest he stir up rebellion, and afraid to kill him lest the people, who thought him a prophet, riot. John would never promise to give up his public work if freed, and Herodias, Herod’s unlawful wife, hated him bitterly. Herod talked with him several times about the kingdom of heaven and was sometimes seriously impressed.
135.b48.p: At Herod’s birthday feast the daughter of Herodias danced, and Herod, well under the influence of wine, promised her anything she asked. Prompted by her mother, she asked for the head of John the Baptist. Herod was filled with fear and sorrow, but because of his oath and his guests he would not refuse. That night John was beheaded in the prison, and his disciples took his body, laid it in a tomb, and went and told Jesus.
135.b50.p: Paper 135 follows the whole life of John the Baptist. Vowed as a Nazarite for life, he tended sheep in the wilderness while reading Daniel and Malachi, and then appeared at the Jordan in Elijah’s garb, calling all Israel to repent. He never saw clearly what the coming kingdom would be like, yet he never wavered in his certainty that it was coming. After baptizing Jesus he accepted that his own work was ending and stepped back into the place of the bridegroom’s friend who rejoices at his voice. In the long darkness of prison, what steadied his faltering faith was Jesus’ word that he had not been forgotten. To prepare the way and then gladly decrease — that was the mission John fulfilled.
135.b51.t: At fourteen he became a Nazarite for life and took up Elijah’s garb
On Jesus’ counsel he cared for his mother and waited for the Father’s hour
Reading Daniel in the wilderness, he came to believe he would herald a new age
Held back by Malachi’s promise, he finally put his doubts aside
Each listener awaited the kingdom of heaven with a different meaning
He baptized Jews for repentance and stirred more than a hundred thousand
Confused in mind, but never in spirit
At the baptism a heavenly voice proclaimed the Son
Neither Elijah nor the Messiah, John pointed to the one to come
Lonely and relieved of his charge, he kept preaching
He must increase, but I must decrease
A drunken oath and bitter hatred took the prophet’s life
135.b53.box: John lived as the voice that prepares the way, then gladly decreased as the bridegroom’s friend — and in that humility his mission was fulfilled.
136.title: Baptism and the Forty Days
136.b0.ask: “With all power in heaven and on earth in his hands, why did Jesus set aside miracles and shortcuts and always choose his Father’s will?”
136.b2.p: Paper 135 showed us the life of John the Baptist and the baptism in the Jordan as John saw it. Paper 136 looks at the same baptism, and the forty days that followed, from Jesus’ side. Jesus began his public work at the height of popular interest in John’s preaching, when the Jews of Palestine were eagerly looking for the Messiah.
136.b3.p: The two men were very different. John was an eager and earnest worker; Jesus was a calm and happy laborer. John’s message was: Repent! flee from the wrath to come. Jesus still called men to repentance, but that call was always followed by the gospel — the good tidings of the joy and liberty of the new kingdom. Jesus spoke of John as the greatest of the prophets of the old order, yet said that the least of those who entered the kingdom of heaven was greater than John.
136.b4.p: What happened at the baptism, and what decisions about his coming ministry did Jesus make during the forty days in the hills of Perea?
136.b5.q: ⟦Q 136:10.1⟧And in all other matters, as in these now of decision-record, I pledge you I will be subject to the will of my Father.⟦/Q⟧
136.b8.p: The Jews held many ideas about the coming deliverer, and each school could point to passages of scripture to support its view. The names they gave him changed over time, but all agreed that he would be the Messiah, “⟦Q 136:1.1|98:7.2|157:5.1⟧the anointed one.⟦/Q⟧” The more learned Jews pictured him as the perfected Israelite, combining in himself the threefold office of prophet, priest, and king.
136.b9.t: The earlier prophets — a human Messiah
Daniel and some later prophets — a superhuman Messiah
The author of the Book of Enoch and his contemporaries
136.b10.p: The rabbis had gathered nearly five hundred passages they believed foretold the Messiah, but amid all the details of time and method they almost completely lost sight of his personality. They were looking for Israel’s temporal glory rather than the salvation of the world. Above all, they never imagined the union of the human and the divine in one person. The incarnation of the Creator in the form of the creature was revealed only in Jesus.
136.b12.p: The Jews believed that the sin of one individual might curse the whole nation, so many devout people were baptized by John for the good of Israel. Jesus did not receive baptism as a rite of repentance or for the remission of sins; he simply followed the example of these pious Israelites. When he stood in the Jordan that day, he was a perfected mortal who had reached the pinnacle of human ascension in the conquest of mind and in self-identification with the spirit.
136.b13.p: Many superhuman observers expected to see the fusion of Jesus with his Adjuster, but something new and even greater happened. As John laid his hands on him, the indwelling Adjuster took final leave of Jesus’ perfected human soul, and a few moments later returned from Divinington as a Personalized Adjuster. It was this Adjuster’s voice, speaking for the Universal Father, that was heard. When Jesus prayed, “⟦Q 136:2.4⟧the heavens were opened,⟦/Q⟧” and he saw a vision of himself as a Son of God before his incarnation and as he would be when it was finished.
136.b14.t: The voice: “⟦Q 136:2.3|135:8.6|135:9.7⟧This is my beloved Son⟦/Q⟧”
Jesus, John, and Jesus’ two brothers
The vision when the heavens opened
John’s disciples at the water’s edge
136.b15.q: ⟦Q 136:2.7⟧The divine Son has found his Father, the Universal Father has found his incarnated Son, and they speak the one to the other.⟦/Q⟧
136.b16.p: This day of baptism ended the purely human life of Jesus. He was almost thirty-one and a half years old, and it was A.D. 26 — the fifteenth year of the actual rule of Tiberius.
136.b18.p: Before his baptism, on Mount Hermon, Jesus had met and defeated Caligastia alone, and on the universe records he had become the Planetary Prince of Urantia. The forty days of retirement after the baptism were not for fasting or afflicting his soul. Jesus was not an ascetic; he came to destroy forever all such notions about the approach to God. He went apart to adjust himself to the changed relationships brought about by the personalization of his Adjuster, and to plan the methods of his new phase of life.
136.b19.p: In the hills Jesus met Gabriel, and then the Constellation Father of Edentia appeared to declare that his sovereignty was complete.
136.b20.t: Word that his universe sovereignty and the end of the Lucifer rebellion were practically achieved
The records were completed, and he brought Immanuel’s bestowal release
Your course from now on is a matter of your own choosing
136.b22.p: Jesus first decided not to teach at the same time as John, but to remain in comparative retirement until John’s work was done. Remembering Immanuel’s instruction to leave no permanent writing on the planet, he never again wrote on anything except sand, and on his next visit to Nazareth he destroyed all his writing that had been preserved there. He did not fast during these forty days, and he was not tempted by any evil spirits.
136.b23.p: Gabriel reminded Jesus that, if he chose to stay on Urantia, there were two ways in which he might live out the rest of his life. His choice between them would have nothing to do with his universe sovereignty.
136.b24.t: What seemed most pleasant and profitable for the immediate needs of this world
A farseeing ideal of creature life visualized by the Paradise administration
136.b25.p: On the third day of his isolation Jesus promised himself that he would go back to finish his earth career, and that whenever two ways lay before him he would always choose the Father’s will. He kept this resolve to the bitter end. These forty days were not a period of great temptation but of the Master’s great decisions. From this time on his spiritualized human mind always said, “⟦Q 136:4.4|109:6.5|111:5.6⟧Not my will but yours be done.⟦/Q⟧”
136.b27.p: On the third day Jesus was shown the celestial hosts of Nebadon assembled to wait on his will — twelve legions of seraphim and representatives of every order of universe intelligence. The first great decision was whether he would use these mighty personalities in his public work. He decided not to use a single one unless it became evident that this was his Father’s will, and he placed them under the command of his Personalized Adjuster.
136.b28.p: The Adjuster explained one limit. Because a Personalized Adjuster is a nontime being, he could fully restrain the hosts in matters of space but not in matters of time. So whatever supernatural element appeared in Jesus’ ministry had to do with the elimination of time, and to avoid apparent time miracles Jesus had to remain constantly time conscious.
136.b29.t: If Jesus entertained a definite desire, time was abridged and it was done at once
136.b31.p: By the third day Jesus’ body was hungry. Should he go in search of food like any ordinary man, or simply use his creative power to produce it? This decision was later portrayed as a temptation to “⟦Q 136:6.1⟧command that these stones become loaves of bread.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus chose to follow the path of normal earthly existence for his personal needs and not to transcend or violate the natural laws he himself had established — a choice that amounted to deciding against miracles and wonders.
136.b32.p: He decided not to seek self-preservation, and he summed up his conclusion in the words of Scripture: “⟦Q 136:6.4⟧Man shall not live by bread alone but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.⟦/Q⟧” He might use his superhuman power for others, but for himself, never — and he held to this even on the cross, when it was jeeringly said, “⟦Q 136:6.5⟧He saved others; himself he cannot save.⟦/Q⟧”
136.b33.q: ⟦Q 136:6.8⟧He came to reveal his Father in heaven to his children on earth, while he sought to lead his earth children to join him in a sincere effort so to live as to do the will of the Father in heaven.⟦/Q⟧
136.b34.p: To sell God-given abilities for personal glory or selfish gain was the very sin of Lucifer and Caligastia. Selfish satisfaction and sensuous gratification cannot by themselves bring happiness; human talents should be devoted chiefly to the growth of mind and spirit.
136.b36.p: The third decision concerned his attitude toward personal danger. Jesus decided to take normal care of his safety and reasonable precautions, but to refrain from all superhuman intervention when the crisis of his life should come. As he thought this through he sat on a ledge above a precipice, knowing he could throw himself off and the celestial hosts could keep him from harm. But such defiance of the Father’s law of gravity would be, not a revelation of the Father, but a questionable trifling with the laws of the universe.
136.b37.p: Jesus therefore never walked on the water nor did anything else that outraged the material order of the world — except, of course, where he could not wholly control the element of time. Whether the Pharisees taunted him for a sign or the watchers at Calvary dared him to come down from the cross, he never departed from the decision of that hour.
136.b39.p: The fourth decision was whether to use his superhuman powers to attract attention and win followers. Jesus ruled out every such method of making his mission known. Even when he allowed time-shortening acts of mercy, he almost always told those he healed to tell no one. He saw that wonders would call forth only outward allegiance by overawing the material mind; they would neither reveal God nor save men.
136.b40.p: His human mind did have some questioning: without wonders the Jews would never accept him as the Messiah. But Jesus decided that the divine mind should not make this concession to the doubting human mind. He also refused all compromise with the wisdom of the world and the influence of riches, and he set aside shortcuts such as walking out on the air from the pinnacle of the temple at Passover. He chose to establish the kingdom by natural, ordinary, difficult, and trying methods.
136.b42.p: The fifth decision concerned the methods of proclaiming and establishing the kingdom of God. Jesus now ceased to regard himself as the Jewish Messiah as that Messiah was popularly conceived. The kingdom of heaven had to do with the overthrow of evil in human hearts — it was purely spiritual — so he rejected any plan to inaugurate it with a dazzling display of power. He proclaimed to an onlooking universe, “⟦Q 136:9.3⟧You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.⟦/Q⟧”
136.b43.t: Dealing out bread to the multitudes
He would not cater to people’s physical gratification
He would not be the miracle deliverer the Jews expected
He would not win acceptance of a spiritual message by power
136.b44.p: He had the power to take the kingdoms of this world, but he did not want them. His only aim was to reveal God to man and to establish the rule of the heavenly Father in human hearts. Knowing that this choice meant the Jews would finally reject him, he long tried to keep his early followers from calling him the Messiah. Throughout his public ministry he faced the clamor to be fed, the insistence on miracles, and the request to make him king, but he never departed from the decisions he made in these hills.
136.b46.p: On the last day of his isolation, before going down to join John and his disciples, Jesus made his final decision and declared it to his Personalized Adjuster: in all other matters, as in those he had now decided, he would be subject to the will of his Father. Then he came down the mountain, and his face shone with the glory of spiritual victory and moral achievement.
136.b47.t: The decisions of the forty days
Not to use the universe hosts unless the Father willed it
Not to use his power for his own needs
To rule out superhuman intervention in personal danger
Not to win followers by miracles and signs
To establish the kingdom by spiritual means, not by power
To be subject to the Father’s will in all things
136.b49.p: Paper 136 shows how the whole direction of Jesus’ public ministry was set at his baptism and in the forty days that followed. At the baptism his purely human life ended, and the Personalized Adjuster was with him from then on. He could now command the universe hosts, turn stones into bread, throw himself from a cliff, or win a nation with wonders and power. But in the hills of Perea he laid down every one of these shortcuts. He would not use his power for himself, and he would build the Father’s kingdom in human hearts by the natural, slow, and sure way. These forty days were not a time of temptation but of decision, and all his decisions came together in one pledge: always to choose the Father’s will.
136.b50.t: No one had imagined the human and divine united in one person
The Adjuster returned personalized, and his purely human life ended
Not a time of fasting, but of adjusting and planning
He resolved to choose the Father’s way, not his own
He would not use the universe hosts unless the Father willed it
His power might serve others, but never himself
Even in danger he would not trifle with natural law
He would not win people by miracles and signs
The kingdom is built by spiritual means, not by power
He pledged to be subject to the Father’s will in all things
136.b52.box: By laying aside every power and shortcut and always choosing the Father’s will, Jesus showed the whole universe the way the kingdom of heaven is built.
137.title: Tarrying Time in Galilee
137.b0.ask: “Why did Jesus, having gathered his first disciples, wait four months and teach that the kingdom comes not by wonders but by a change of heart?”
137.b2.p: In Paper 136 Jesus, after his baptism, spent forty days alone in the hills deciding how he would carry out his mission. Now Paper 137 shows the first time those decisions were tested among people. Early on Saturday morning, February 23, A.D. 26, Jesus came down from the hills and rejoined John’s company encamped at Pella. That same day he cared for a boy who had been hurt in a fall and took him safely home to his parents.
137.b3.p: The paper follows one event after another: the choosing of the first six apostles, the turning of water into wine at the wedding in Cana, four months of waiting and training in Capernaum, and the first public sermon on the kingdom of God. All along, people waited for some astonishing sign. Again and again Jesus asked them instead to wait upon the will of the Father.
137.b4.p: Why, then, did Jesus choose to wait when everyone around him expected wonders? And where does the kingdom he proclaimed come from?
137.b5.q: “⟦Q 137:8.9⟧And this kingdom is even now among you, for where the spirit of God teaches and leads the soul of man, there in reality is the kingdom of heaven.⟦/Q⟧”
137.b8.p: Of all John’s followers, Andrew was the most deeply impressed with Jesus. He made up his mind to follow him, and Jesus welcomed him as the first of the twelve apostles. Andrew’s brother Simon first went to consult John. Though saddened at losing them, John let them go, saying bravely, “⟦Q 137:1.3⟧This is but the beginning.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus praised Simon’s enthusiasm but warned him to be more thoughtful in his speech, and he changed his name to Peter.
137.b9.p: James and John, the sons of Zebedee, had spent days searching the hills for Jesus. When they came back, they were hurt that others had been chosen first. Jesus told them to look for the secret of the kingdom in their hearts rather than in the hills, and he assured them that they had belonged to the kingdom even before they asked. From then on the two brothers were never again envious of Andrew and Simon. And from that day the word “apostle” was used to set apart the chosen family of Jesus’ advisers from the great multitude of believing disciples.
137.b10.t: Decided on his own to follow and asked Jesus to receive him
Urged by Andrew; joined after consulting John
Counted as already belonging to the kingdom
137.b11.q: “⟦Q 137:1.6⟧You should learn to search for the secret of the new kingdom in your hearts and not in the hills.⟦/Q⟧”
137.b13.p: On February 24 Jesus said good-bye to John the Baptist; he never saw him again in the flesh. That day the first great division broke out among John’s followers. Ezra declared that a Galilean carpenter could not be the Deliverer. He left with many disciples, and they formed a sect of those who believed in John but refused to accept Jesus.
137.b14.p: On the road to Galilee, Philip of Bethsaida came up with his friend Nathaniel. When Philip asked whether he should go down to John, Jesus answered, “Follow me.” Nathaniel, hearing the news from Philip, was startled: “⟦Q 137:2.6⟧Can any such good thing come out of Nazareth?⟦/Q⟧” Philip only said, “⟦Q 137:2.6|139:5.8|168:1.1⟧Come and see.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus received this sincere doubter, calling him “⟦Q 137:2.7⟧a genuine Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.⟦/Q⟧”
137.b15.t: Rejected him — a carpenter could not be the Deliverer — and left
At the words “Follow me,” he was sure he had found the Deliverer
Doubted at first, but after seeing Jesus called him “⟦Q 137:2.7|141:3.4⟧a master of men⟦/Q⟧”
137.b16.p: With this, Jesus had gathered half of his associates. That night, in his boyhood home at Nazareth, he destroyed every trace of his writing that remained about the house. His disciples were deeply impressed that they never afterward saw him write — except upon the dust or in the sand.
137.b18.p: The new associates told Jesus’ family about the recent events, and even his brother Joseph said: “⟦Q 137:3.2⟧Maybe, after all, Mother was right — maybe our strange brother is the coming king.⟦/Q⟧” His friends in Capernaum saw a great and pleasant change in him. In the years around his baptism he had grown more and more serious and self-contained; now he was once again lighthearted and joyful.
137.b19.p: Mary was thrilled, believing that Gabriel’s promise was soon to be fulfilled. Jesus warned everyone again and again to tell no one about him, but his family and disciples were convinced that he would show his authority as the Messiah at the wedding in Cana, and they quietly spread the word. Mary set out for Cana in the spirit of a queen mother on the way to see her son crowned.
137.b21.p: By noon on Wednesday nearly a thousand guests had arrived in Cana — more than four times the number invited. Mary and James came to ask Jesus at what point he would reveal himself as the “supernatural one.” He said only that if they loved him, they should be willing to tarry with him while he waited upon the will of his Father. To make an outward show of his divinity was exactly what he had decided not to do in the hills. When the wine ran out and Mary pleaded with him again, Jesus answered, “⟦Q 137:4.8⟧We must in all things wait upon the will of the Father in heaven.⟦/Q⟧”
137.b22.p: Then, as his mother stood weeping before him, the human heart of Jesus was overcome with compassion. He began to say that he would gladly do what she asked if it were part of the Father’s will — and stopped short. But he had already desirefully thought too much. Wine appeared in the six stone jars nearby, and of everyone at the feast, Jesus himself was the most surprised. All the required personalities were assembled, and his Adjuster had signified that this was in no way against the Father’s will; so, in the face of the wish of the Universe Creator Sovereign, there was no escaping the appearance of the wine.
137.b23.t: None was modified, abrogated, or transcended
Time was abrogated, and the chemical elements were assembled by celestial agencies
The wine was made just as by the ordinary natural processes
It could happen because it did not contravene his will
137.b24.q: ⟦Q 137:4.13⟧But this was in no sense a miracle. No law of nature was modified, abrogated, or even transcended.⟦/Q⟧
137.b25.p: Now everyone believed in him as the Messiah. But Jesus was sorely perplexed, knowing that they believed only because of an unusual event. He saw that he must constantly be on guard lest his sympathy and pity lead to repeated episodes of this sort.
137.b27.p: At dawn the next day Jesus left with his six apostles for Zebedee’s home in Bethsaida without saying good-bye, and he warned them not to speak of the water and the wine. That evening, when he set out to make clear who he was and how his mission might end, the apostles were stunned and speechless. His brother Jude confessed that, though he had never understood him, he had heard the voice at the Jordan and believed in him no matter who he was.
137.b28.p: That night Jesus sat on the lake shore thinking until dawn. He came to see that he would never be able to make his followers see him in any light other than as the long-expected Messiah. He was not the Davidic type of Messiah, yet he truly fulfilled the words of the more spiritually minded of the ancient prophets. Never again did he wholly deny that he was the Messiah. Then he sent the apostles back to their nets, to wait until John’s work was finished.
137.b29.h: 6. The Events of a Sabbath Day
137.b30.p: Jesus’ first public appearance after his baptism came on March 2, A.D. 26, in the synagogue at Capernaum. The place was crowded with people hoping for some supernatural display, but the hope went unfulfilled. Jesus read from Isaiah, said simply, “⟦Q 137:6.3⟧Be patient and you shall see the glory of God,⟦/Q⟧” and sat down.
137.b31.p: That afternoon, in a boat, Jesus told his apostles to go on with their daily work until the hour of the kingdom came and to spend three hours every evening in study. His kingdom, he said, would come not with noise and glamor but through a great change in their hearts. He warned them to be ready for trouble as well as joy.
137.b32.t: Return to your accustomed work as if nothing had happened
Spend three hours every evening in study and preparation
Be patient, be gentle, be ever obedient to the Father’s will
Be prepared for much tribulation as well as great joy
137.b34.p: From March through June Jesus held more than a hundred long, earnest, and cheerful sessions with his six associates and his brother James. Nothing miraculous happened at all, and Mary’s faith sank to new low levels. Yet these seven believers learned that it was really easy to be “⟦Q 137:7.2⟧friends with God.⟦/Q⟧” When Peter pressed to begin preaching, Jesus always answered, “⟦Q 137:7.3⟧Be patient, Simon. Make progress.⟦/Q⟧”
137.b35.p: During this time Jesus taught them how to regard the various groups of Palestine. His words were always, “⟦Q 137:7.5⟧We are seeking to win all of them, but we are not of any of them.⟦/Q⟧” Every party looked for a national deliverer, but from the start Jesus taught that the kingdom of heaven is a spiritual experience — the enthronement of God in the hearts of men.
137.b36.t: Scribes and rabbis; a progressive group that accepted the resurrection of the dead
Priests and wealthy Jews; less strict about the details of the law
Arose during the Maccabean revolt; a monastic brotherhood holding property in common
Held that any means was justified to escape the Roman yoke
A political party seeking the restoration of Herod’s dynasty
In central Palestine; beliefs similar to Judaism
137.b37.p: The apostles later remembered these four months as the most precious and profitable time of all their association with the Master. Jesus taught them only as much as they could take in, and he did not confuse them with truths beyond their grasp.
137.b39.p: When Peter brought news of John’s arrest, Jesus laid down his tools and said, “⟦Q 137:8.2⟧The Father’s hour has come.⟦/Q⟧” June 18, A.D. 26, was his last day at the carpenter’s bench. On the Sabbath, June 22, in the synagogue at Capernaum, he preached his sermon on the kingdom — the first major public declaration of his career.
137.b40.p: He announced that this kingdom would include the worshiping souls of Jew and gentile, rich and poor, free and bond. It would be founded not by armies or worldly glory; his disciples would enter it by their moral decisions and their spirit victories. John had preached repentance, but Jesus proclaimed faith, the gift of God, as the price of entrance into the kingdom.
137.b41.t: “⟦Q 137:8.7|138:7.1|152:3.2⟧My kingdom is not of this world.⟦/Q⟧”
The faith and trusting dependence of a little child
Where the spirit of God teaches and leads the soul of man
He who would be great must first become server of all
Like a seed in good soil, it ripens over time
Faith that the Father loves you with an infinite love
137.b42.p: Of those who heard him, about one third believed though they could not fully understand; about one third prepared to reject so purely spiritual an idea of the kingdom; and the remaining third could not grasp his teaching, many thinking he “⟦Q 137:8.18|100:7.12|126:3.13⟧was beside himself.⟦/Q⟧”
137.b44.p: Paper 137 is the story of how Jesus chose to wait at a time when everyone was waiting for signs. The first apostles were called each in a different way, and even what happened at Cana was not what Jesus wanted. He accepted that he could not change, all at once, the messianic hopes that gathered around him, and for four quiet months he stayed with his disciples, teaching them as much as they could absorb. Only when John’s work was done did he proclaim the kingdom. It is a kingdom entered not by armies or wonders but by faith in the Father’s love — a kingdom already present in every heart the spirit of God is leading.
137.b45.t: The secret of the kingdom is found in the heart, not in the hills
With the words “Follow me,” half the associates were gathered
His family and disciples expected him to show his messianic authority
The wine was an abrogation of time, not a breaking of natural law
Jesus accepted the messianic hope and left its untangling to the Father
6. The Events of a Sabbath Day
The kingdom comes not with noise but through a great change of heart
Belonging to no party, he quietly prepared his disciples
The spiritual kingdom, entered by faith, was first publicly proclaimed
137.b47.q: ⟦Q 137:8.17⟧If you would but believe that my Father loves you with an infinite love, then you are in the kingdom of God.⟦/Q⟧
138.title: Training the Kingdom’s Messengers
138.b0.ask: “Why did Jesus train his twelve apostles first through quiet personal work and fishing rather than through public preaching?”
138.b2.p: In Paper 137 Jesus proclaimed the kingdom of God publicly for the first time, in the synagogue at Capernaum. Now Paper 138 shows how the messengers of that kingdom were gathered and trained. On the afternoon after the sermon, Jesus told his six apostles of his plan to visit the cities around the Sea of Galilee. His brothers James and Jude were not invited to the meeting, and they were deeply hurt.
138.b3.p: Jesus had decided not to include his close kin among the leaders of the apostolic group. This decision, along with the distance he kept from his mother after Cana, was the beginning of a widening gap between Jesus and his family. That gap was not fully closed until after the resurrection; only Ruth, the youngest, never once wavered in her loyalty to her brother.
138.b4.p: Why, then, did Jesus, holding unlimited power, prepare his disciples in the quietest and least dramatic way? And what did that training leave with them?
138.b5.q: ⟦Q 138:8.9⟧Nothing ever seemed so important to Jesus as the individual human who chanced to be in his immediate presence.⟦/Q⟧
138.b8.p: On June 23, A.D. 26, Jesus sent the six apostles out two by two. He forbade them to baptize and advised against public preaching. Their first tour was to be entirely one of personal work, so that they could gain experience in dealing personally with their fellow men. Jesus also announced that he would appoint twelve apostles, and he asked each of the six to choose one man from among the early believers.
138.b10.p: While the apostles were away, Jesus visited his family in Nazareth and did everything humanly possible to keep their love and confidence. He felt a strong temptation to use his power to free John from prison, but once again he waited upon the Father’s will.
138.b12.p: The first missionary tour was a great success. The apostles discovered the great value of direct, personal contact with people, and they came to see more clearly that religion is, after all, purely a matter of personal experience. Each of them then nominated a candidate, the others voted, and all six were unanimously accepted.
138.b13.t: Fisherman of Tarichea; once a carpenter and stone mason
Twin brother of James Alpheus; a fisherman
High officer of the Zealots; formerly a merchant
Only son of a wealthy family of Jericho; the only Judean
138.b14.h: 3. The Call of Matthew and Simon
138.b15.p: At the customs house Jesus said to Matthew, “Follow me,” and Matthew rose and followed. Then Peter presented Simon Zelotes, and Jesus called him with the same words. That evening, at the banquet in Matthew’s home, many of the guests were people the Pharisees would call “⟦Q 138:3.4|138:3.6|121:8.8⟧publicans and sinners,⟦/Q⟧” and the Pharisees looking on began to criticize Jesus in their hearts.
138.b16.p: Jesus answered that he had come to proclaim joy to the socially downtrodden and spiritual liberty to the moral captives. Andrew afterward persuaded Simon not to make speeches, so that the kingdom would not be confused with the Zealot movement.
138.b17.q: “⟦Q 138:3.6⟧They who are whole need not a physician, but rather those who are sick? I have come, not to call the righteous, but sinners.⟦/Q⟧”
138.b19.p: James and Judas, the twin sons of Alpheus, were waiting on the beach at Kheresa, and they too heard the call: “Follow me.” That afternoon Jesus taught that the kingdom of heaven is open to all men and women. They were not to refuse to break bread with Pharisee or sinner, Roman or Jew, rich or poor.
138.b20.p: That night Jesus taught them, for the first time, about the origin, nature, and destiny of unclean spirits, but they did not understand. They found it easy to love Jesus, but hard to understand his teachings.
138.b21.h: 5. The Call of Thomas and Judas
138.b22.p: At Tarichea Jesus told Thomas that he lacked faith but received him nonetheless. To Judas Iscariot he said that he prayed Judas would always be loyal to his Galilean brethren, and then: “Follow me.” With the twelve now together, Jesus taught them about the nature and work of the Holy Spirit. But they kept making the mistake of trying to fit the new gospel into the mold of their old beliefs.
138.b23.p: In Zebedee’s home at Capernaum, Jesus urged them to avoid any clash with the civil authorities: “⟦Q 138:5.4⟧If the civil rulers are to be rebuked, leave that task to me.⟦/Q⟧” That same evening Judas Iscariot asked why nothing was being done to get John out of prison, and he was not wholly satisfied with Jesus’ attitude.
138.b25.p: During the following week each new apostle spent his days reviewing the teachings so far with the apostle who had nominated him, and in the evenings they all gathered in Zebedee’s garden to hear Jesus. At this time Jesus set aside Wednesday of each week as a day of rest and recreation. He did not himself need it, but he knew it was best for his human associates.
138.b26.p: He urged them not to wander off into preaching about him or building legends and cults about his person, but to proclaim the gospel of the kingdom and the revelation of the Father. He avoided controversies, except where wrong ideas of the Father were concerned, and although he held unlimited power, he insisted on the quietest way of all.
138.b27.q: “⟦Q 138:6.4⟧Go seek for the sinners; find the downhearted and comfort the anxious.⟦/Q⟧”
138.b29.p: Peter, James, and Judas Iscariot came to ask when the kingdom would be set up and what position each of them would hold. Jesus told them to give up the idea of a reign of power and glory, for he had called them as ambassadors of a spiritual kingdom. The apostles went off two by two to pray, and when they came back they pledged their unchanging loyalty to the kingdom — even though, as Thomas admitted, they did not fully understand it.
138.b30.p: When it turned out that they had not even enough money to last two weeks, Jesus planned for them to fish for two weeks and then do personal work for two weeks, and he let them organize themselves under Andrew’s leadership. As Matthew said one day: “⟦Q 138:7.6⟧Of this man, even the less I comprehend him, the more I love him.⟦/Q⟧” This plan went on for more than five months.
138.b32.p: In mid-August the apostles went out two by two, and Jesus went once with each pair in the order in which they had been chosen. He taught that sins are forgiven through faith in God, without penance or sacrifice, and that the Father loves all his children with the same eternal love.
138.b33.t: The work and imprisonment of John the Baptist
The voice heard at the baptism
Only those who heard it may mention it; never repeat hearsay
The water and wine at Cana
138.b34.p: Jesus made plain the difference between repentance through so-called good works and the change of mind by faith — the new birth. John had urged repentance in order to flee from the wrath to come, but Jesus taught that faith is the open door into the love of God. He showed deep respect for everyone he met; he would interrupt a serious conference to welcome a child, and he made it very clear that women were to be accorded equal rights with men in the kingdom.
138.b35.t: Repent, to flee from the wrath to come
Faith is the open door into God’s love
A change of mind by faith
138.b37.p: This rather monotonous period of alternate fishing and personal work was a grueling test, but the apostles endured it. Because of their personal association with Jesus in these months, all of them except Judas Iscariot remained loyal to him even in the dark hours of the trial and crucifixion. What held them together was not his superb teachings or marvelous doings, but one human sentiment: friendship-loyalty.
138.b38.p: These quiet months were also a severe trial for Jesus’ family. Nearly all of them except Ruth turned away from him and even wanted to bring him home. Meanwhile the apostles worked in many towns and villages — Capernaum, Chorazin, Magdala, Cana, and others — and also made arrangements for the support of their families.
138.b40.p: From early on the apostles organized themselves as follows, and this arrangement lasted until the desertion of Judas made a reorganization necessary.
138.b41.t: Watching over the needs of the apostles’ families
Fiscal agent — keeping the budget and replenishing the funds
Manager of the itinerary — arranging lodging and meeting places
Treasurer — keeping the bag and the accounts
138.b42.p: They went on in this simple way until January 12, A.D. 27, when Jesus formally ordained them as ambassadors of the kingdom and preachers of its glad tidings.
138.b44.p: Paper 138 shows how ordinary was the preparation of the men who were entrusted with a message to change the world. Jesus called a publican, a Zealot, fishermen, and a doubter alike, and he sent them out first not to crowds but to meet people one by one. The apostles, dreaming of power and position, were disappointed again and again. Yet in five months of fishing, resting, and working together, each came to regard Jesus as the best friend he had in all the world. It was that friendship and loyalty that held them fast, later, even in the darkest hour.

2. Choosing the Six

5. The Call of Thomas and Judas
