138.b47.box: Jesus raised up the messengers of the kingdom not by displays of power but by quiet personal ministry and friendship.
139.title: The Twelve Apostles
139.b0.ask: “What did each of these twelve very different men see in Jesus that held them to him to the end?”
139.b2.p: In Paper 138 we saw how the twelve apostles were gathered and organized. Now Paper 139 brings each of the twelve into close view, one by one. Jesus repeatedly dashed their hopes and tore up their ambitions for personal exaltation, yet only one of them deserted him. That fact is an eloquent testimony to the charm and righteousness of his life on earth.
139.b3.p: The apostles learned about the kingdom of heaven from Jesus, and Jesus learned a great deal about human nature from them. They should not be thought of as ignorant and unlearned men. All except the Alpheus twins were graduates of the synagogue schools; they simply had not been trained in the traditions and methods of interpretation of the rabbis.
139.b4.p: What, then, drew these twelve men, so different in temperament and background, to Jesus? And how did knowing him change them?
139.b5.q: ⟦Q 139:9.8⟧Jesus does not look down upon littleness, only upon evil and sin.⟦/Q⟧
139.b8.p: Andrew, at thirty-three, was the oldest of the twelve and the ablest man among them, equal to any of his fellows in nearly every way except oratory. A fine administrator, he served as chairman of the apostolic corps to the end. He was the best judge of men in the group, and he was the first to sense that trouble was brewing in the heart of Judas Iscariot.
139.b9.p: He was never in the least jealous of his eloquent brother Peter. When two thousand souls were added to the kingdom through Peter’s preaching at Pentecost, Andrew said, “⟦Q 139:1.6⟧I could not do that, but I am glad I have a brother who could.⟦/Q⟧” His weakness was a lack of enthusiasm, which made him slow to praise his associates. He admired Jesus’ consistent sincerity and unaffected dignity. Later, at Patrae in Achaia, he was crucified, and for two full days he went on preaching from the cross until he died.
139.b11.p: Peter was thirty years old and married. Impulsive and optimistic, he was always in trouble because he spoke before he thought. A born leader, fluent and dramatic, he asked more questions than all the other apostles put together. What he most admired in Jesus was his supernal tenderness — his teaching that one should forgive even seventy times seven.
139.b12.p: He was brave in the face of open attack but shrank before ridicule; at the taunts of a serving maid he denied his Master. Jesus knew that Peter’s fault lay in his head, not in his heart. Once he was sure he had been forgiven, Peter became a light of salvation to thousands, and in Rome he counted it a great honor to be crucified like his Master.
139.b14.p: James, the elder of the two “⟦Q 139:3.1|139:3.5|181:2.4⟧sons of thunder,⟦/Q⟧” was thirty. His anger, once aroused, was fierce, but otherwise he was much like Andrew, and he was second only to Peter as a public speaker. He had a rare gift for seeing many sides of a question, and of all the twelve he came nearest to grasping the real meaning of Jesus’ teaching.
139.b15.p: He most admired the sympathetic affection of Jesus, and he was a fine balance wheel for Peter. When Jesus asked whether he was able to drink the cup, his answer that he was ready proved literally true. He was put to death with the sword by Herod Agrippa, the first of the apostles to die a martyr.
139.b17.p: John, the youngest at twenty-four, acted as Jesus’ personal agent in dealing with his family. Still, it cannot truly be said that he was “⟦Q 139:4.2|139:4.4⟧the disciple whom Jesus loved,⟦/Q⟧” for it is hard to imagine so large-minded a personality as Jesus playing favorites. John’s weakness was a well-hidden conceit; his strength was that he was thoroughly dependable.
139.b18.p: The love and unselfishness of Jesus came to rule the rest of his life, and the “⟦Q 139:4.6⟧son of thunder⟦/Q⟧” became the “⟦Q 139:4.6⟧apostle of love.⟦/Q⟧” He was the only apostle who followed straight after Jesus on the night of his arrest, and the first to believe fully in the resurrection. He wrote the Book of Revelation while in exile on Patmos, became the ablest theologian among them, and died a natural death at Ephesus at the age of one hundred and one.
139.b21.p: Philip, the twenty-seven-year-old steward, always wanted to be “shown.” He was an ordinary man, lacking imagination, but methodical and thorough; for four years he provided food for everyone with hardly a lapse. Jesus never once rebuked him for the foolish questions he asked in the middle of a profound discourse, for he knew that a rebuke would keep this honest soul from ever asking freely again.
139.b22.p: Philip had the rare gift of saying not “Go” but “Come.” That is always the effective technique in all forms and phases of teaching, and even parents may learn from it. He revered Jesus’ unfailing generosity. He became the first to win souls outside the Jewish fold, and at last he was crucified and buried at Hierapolis.
139.b24.p: Nathaniel, twenty-five, was the youngest child of a family and supported his aging parents; with Judas Iscariot he was the best educated of the twelve. His great virtue was an honesty without guile; his weakness was a pride and prejudice that judged people in advance. Yet he was not stubborn — one look at Jesus’ face, and he changed his mind.
139.b25.p: He was the philosopher and storyteller of the group, and when tension rose he eased it with flashes of humor. When Judas complained about him, Jesus answered that it is not the Father’s will that his children should partake only of the serious things of life. Nathaniel revered Jesus’ tolerance above all. He went to Mesopotamia and India to preach the gospel and died in India.
139.b27.p: Matthew, a thirty-one-year-old customs collector of Capernaum, was the only man of means in the group. That he, a publican, had been accepted was a source of overwhelming gratitude to him, and what he valued most in Jesus was his forgiving disposition. His notes later became the basis of the Gospel of Matthew, written by Isador.
139.b28.p: He gave practically all his wealth to the work, but he gave it in the names of other believers for fear his fellows would consider the money tainted. When he was looked down upon, he bore it quietly and never revealed his generosity; the apostles died without ever learning that he had been their benefactor. Because he was among the twelve, the doors of the kingdom stayed open to multitudes of souls who had thought themselves outcasts.
139.b30.p: Thomas, twenty-nine, a former carpenter and stone mason, was the scientist of the group — the only one of the twelve with a truly analytical mind. An unhappy childhood had left him with a suspicious and pessimistic temperament, yet the better his fellows knew him, the more they liked him, and they found him supremely honest and loyal. His presence among the twelve was a standing declaration that Jesus loved even honest doubters.
139.b31.p: In council he argued for caution, but once a decision was made, he was the first to cry, “Let’s go!” — a good loser. He revered Jesus’ superbly balanced character, at once merciful and just, strong and gentle. Thomas is the great example of a man who doubts, faces his doubts, and wins; a man who would have left at the first sign of fraud believed in Jesus to the end. He was put to death in Malta.
139.b32.t: The balance Thomas saw in Jesus
139.b33.q: ⟦Q 139:8.12⟧Thomas is the great example of a human being who has doubts, faces them, and wins.⟦/Q⟧
139.b35.p: The Alpheus twins were ordinary fishermen of twenty-six who managed the crowds; they were the odd-job men and errand boys of the apostolic group. They hardly understood the philosophical discussions, but they rejoiced to know themselves the least of all the apostles. Seeing two men like themselves in places of honor, countless timid believers were encouraged to enter the kingdom.
139.b36.p: James loved Jesus’ simplicity, and Judas his unostentatious humility. They were loyal to the end and, after John, were among the first to believe in the resurrection, but after the crucifixion they went back to their families and their nets. Jesus welcomed these young men of one talent to positions of honor on his personal staff.
139.b38.p: Simon Zelotes, twenty-eight, was a former merchant and a fiery agitator devoted to the Zealots; he took charge of the group’s recreation and play. His strength was an inspiring loyalty that could lead a hesitant person into the joy of faith in about fifteen minutes. But four years was too short a time to turn a Jewish nationalist into a spiritual internationalist.
139.b39.p: He marveled at Jesus’ calmness and his unexplainable poise. Jesus often told him that it was proper to want to see the social order improved, but that this was not the business of the kingdom of heaven; their business was to be ambassadors of a spiritual government. After the persecutions Simon collapsed for a while, but he rose again and carried the gospel into the heart of Africa, where he was buried.
139.b41.p: Judas, born at Kerioth, was thirty and unmarried. His Sadducean parents had disowned him, and he was the only Judean among the twelve. He was an able treasurer and kept his trust honestly until his betrayal; money was never the motive for it. But he never truly understood himself, and there was no trait of Jesus that he especially admired.
139.b42.p: For Jesus, Judas was an adventure in faith, for it is the nature of the Sons of God to give every creature an equal chance of salvation. But when light is not honestly received and lived up to, it tends to become darkness within the soul. Judas brooded over his personal disappointments and resentments, and after being publicly rebuked over the ointment, he decided on revenge. Jesus did everything possible short of interfering with his moral freedom, and he had only pity for his betrayer.
139.b43.t: What he most admired in Jesus
His consistent sincerity and unaffected dignity
Nothing in particular beyond his general charm
139.b45.p: Paper 139 shows that Jesus did not choose perfect men. He took them just as they were — the impulsive and the doubting, a publican and a Zealot, plain fishermen. Each of the twelve was drawn to a different side of Jesus, and each was changed, little by little, by living with him. The son of thunder became the apostle of love; the doubter overcame his doubts; the least of them rejoiced in their place. Even the tragedy of Judas reminds us that the door of eternal life is open to all, but that the light must be received and lived.
139.b46.t: A brother without jealousy, a steady administrator
Impulsive and wavering, yet forgiven and made a great light
The first martyr, who came nearest to Jesus’ meaning
The son of thunder became the apostle of love
A plain steward who led people by saying “⟦Q 139:5.8|137:2.6|168:1.1⟧Come and see⟦/Q⟧”
A guileless philosopher whose humor eased tension
A grateful publican who gave his wealth in secret
An honest scientist who faced his doubts and won
Even the least were given places of honor in the kingdom
A revolutionary turned preacher of peace
Light not received becomes darkness within the soul
139.b48.box: Jesus accepted twelve very different men just as they were, and through his friendship he transformed them.
140.title: The Ordination of the Twelve
140.b0.ask: “Why did Jesus ask his apostles not only to love their neighbors as themselves, but to love men as a father loves his children?”
140.b2.p: In Paper 139 we looked at the temperament and life of each of the twelve apostles. Now Paper 140 tells of the day they were formally set apart as ambassadors of the kingdom. Just before noon on January 12, A.D. 27, Jesus called the apostles together two by two along the shore and led them up into the highlands north of Capernaum. For the first time all twelve were silent; even Peter was lost in thought.
140.b3.p: The paper unfolds the ordination itself, the ordination sermon often called the “⟦Q 140:4.1|140:5.1|140:5.23⟧Sermon on the Mount,⟦/Q⟧” the new idea of fatherly love at its heart, and Jesus’ attitude toward politics, society, and economics. The sermon was not the gospel of Jesus as such; it was the charge he gave to those who would go out to represent him.
140.b4.p: What kind of life, then, did Jesus ask of his representatives? And what was the love that lay at the root of that life?
140.b5.q: ⟦Q 140:1.5⟧This kingdom of which you preach is God within you.⟦/Q⟧
140.b8.p: Before the ordination, Jesus told the apostles seated around him that the Father’s kingdom is an everlasting dominion, and that the Father is neither the God of the Jews nor of the gentiles. The power of this kingdom lies not in armies or riches but in the divine spirit that rules the hearts of the reborn sons of God, and its battle cry is: Peace on earth and good will to all men.
140.b9.p: Faith alone will carry them through the door of the kingdom, but to keep ascending they must bear the fruits of the Father’s spirit. The kingdom does not come with outward show, so they are not to say “⟦Q 140:1.5⟧it is here⟦/Q⟧” or “⟦Q 140:1.5⟧it is there.⟦/Q⟧” And men will know that they have been with Jesus less by their words than by the lives they live.
140.b11.p: Jesus had the twelve kneel in a circle around him, and he laid his hands on the head of each, beginning with Judas Iscariot and ending with Andrew. Then he prayed: as he represented the Father, so he had chosen these men to represent him, and he asked the Father to love them and give them wisdom.
140.b12.p: When the prayer ended, no one spoke; one by one they embraced him. A great silence came over the place while hosts of celestial beings looked down on this scene — the Creator of a universe entrusting the work of the divine brotherhood of man to the minds of men.
140.b14.p: Jesus told them that, now that they had become enlightened citizens of another, heavenly kingdom, it was no longer enough to live as they had lived before. More is required of a teacher than of a pupil, and more of a citizen of the kingdom of heaven than of a citizen of an earthly rule. Then he gave them words of blessing to bring to those in trouble, in two groups.
140.b15.t: The poor in spirit, the humble
Theirs are the treasures of the kingdom of heaven
They who hunger and thirst for righteousness
They shall be called the sons of God
They who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake
Theirs is the kingdom of heaven
140.b16.p: They are the salt of the earth and the light of the world. They are not to resist injustice with force, but to love their enemies and be merciful. They were commissioned to save men, not to judge them. What matters in entering the kingdom is motive; the Father judges by the inner longings and sincere intentions of the heart.
140.b17.h: 4. You Are the Salt of the Earth
140.b18.p: In those days salt was so precious that it served as money. It does its work by seasoning food, preserving it, and making other things taste better. Light drives away darkness, but if it is too dazzling it can confuse; our light should not shine so as to draw attention to ourselves.
140.b19.p: This section sets out a philosophy of living in short statements. Personality is basically changeless; what changes and grows is moral character. The major error of modern religions is negativism, and fear and shame are unworthy motives for religious living. We cannot change our native impulses, but we can change our emotional reactions to them.
140.b20.q: ⟦Q 140:4.6⟧Strong characters are not derived from not doing wrong but rather from actually doing right.⟦/Q⟧
140.b22.p: Brotherly love means loving your neighbor as yourself — the fulfillment of the golden rule. But fatherly love asks that we love our fellows as Jesus loves us. Jesus first set out four attitudes of faith as a prelude, and then explained four supreme reactions of fatherly love that go beyond the limits of brotherly love.
140.b23.t: Humility that is not self-satisfied but seeks truth; its reward comes now
Righteousness is a joy, not a duty — not a matter of “⟦Q 140:4.7|140:5.9|89:2.1⟧thou shalt not⟦/Q⟧”
Not fear, but the cooperation of “⟦Q 140:5.11|111:5.6|118:8.11⟧your will be done⟦/Q⟧”
Free of suspicion and revenge; looks for the best in others
140.b24.t: A tender heart; sympathy is a worthy trait in men and women alike
Fatherliness at its highest — active and dynamic
An active peace that heals distrust and suspicion
The greater love that lays down life for a friend
140.b25.p: The faith and love of these beatitudes strengthen character and create happiness; fear and anger weaken character and destroy happiness. The beatitudes rest not on law or duty but on faith and love, and fatherly love delights in returning good for evil.
140.b27.p: When the apostles failed to understand, Jesus told them it was because they were trying to build the new teaching on top of the old; they must start afresh, like little children. He had come not to destroy the law and the prophets but to fulfill and enlighten them. He looked past the deed to the motive, going back to anger against a brother and the intent to lust after a woman.
140.b28.p: Asked about divorce, Jesus answered that he had come not to legislate but to enlighten. On “⟦Q 140:6.9|140:8.5|70:10.9⟧an eye for an eye,⟦/Q⟧” he said to return good for evil; if this saying was too hard, they could turn back to a less demanding discipleship — but none turned back. That night each apostle had a private talk with Jesus. Finding the twins asleep by the fire, Jesus said, “They are doing well,” and would not let them be wakened.
140.b29.t: I look past the deed to the motive; the Father judges by intent
I have not come to legislate but to enlighten
Nathaniel — an eye for an eye
Return good for evil; mercy determines judgment
Live as one family; seek first the kingdom of God
140.b31.p: When Jesus told them to get ready to go to Jerusalem, Thomas said he feared they were not yet ready and asked to stay a few days longer, and Jesus agreed to remain until the Sabbath. During that week visitors came from Tyre, Sidon, Damascus, and elsewhere, and now it was the apostles who received and taught them.
140.b32.t: Two purposes of the earth mission
To reveal the Father to man
To lead men to become son-conscious
140.b33.p: Some of the apostles grew overconfident and said, “Let us go forth and take the kingdom.” Jesus answered that he hoped their wisdom would equal their zeal. They did not understand all his teaching, but they did not miss the meaning of the beautiful life he lived among them.
140.b35.p: Because the apostles still tried to join the spiritual kingdom to the restoration of David’s throne, Jesus spent four hours on the lake talking with Peter, James, and John. He taught nonresistance, but not passive tolerance of evil-doing. He approved of society punishing criminals and of civil government using force to keep order. His teaching applied to the individual, not to the state.
140.b36.t: Active submission, not fatalism; worry forbidden but forethought allowed
Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s; he was no political reformer
Every man a neighbor; but beware of indiscriminate kindness
The highest human duty, yet it must not stand in the way of religious duty
He warned not against wealth itself but against its unfair distribution and its influence
The willing conformity of man’s will to the will of God
140.b37.p: Were Jesus on earth today, he would take no side in political, social, or economic disputes. He would teach men how to perfect their inner spiritual life so that they could better solve their human problems. His teaching is a religion of boldness and courage; “Fear not” was his watchword. He gave no rules for self-analysis, and he taught not the building of character but its growth — like the mustard seed.
140.b39.p: On the next Sabbath Jesus took the apostles back to the highland where they had been ordained. After a time of talk and fellowship, with no new teaching, he called them before him one by one and commissioned them as his representatives: “⟦Q 140:9.2|100:7.10|193:0.5⟧Freely you have received, freely give.⟦/Q⟧”
140.b40.p: He was sending them out as sheep among wolves, so they must be wise as serpents and harmless as doves. If they were brought before councils and governors, they need not worry about what to say, for the spirit of the Father would speak through them.
140.b42.p: That evening Jesus spoke at length not about what the apostles must do but about what they must be. In the kingdom, being righteous by faith comes before doing righteousness. The apostles kept trying to turn spiritual principles into rules of conduct, but because Jesus himself was everything he taught, they learned bit by bit just by living with him.
140.b43.p: To become like a little child means not credulity but the relationship of a child to its father. When Simon asked whether all men are the sons of God, Jesus said yes, and that this was the good news they were to proclaim. To John he described the three essentials of the kingdom of heaven.
140.b44.t: Recognition of the fact of the sovereignty of God
Belief in the truth of sonship with God
Faith in the supreme human desire to do the will of God — to be like God
140.b45.q: “⟦Q 140:10.7⟧Yes, Simon, all men are the sons of God, and that is the good news you are going to proclaim.⟦/Q⟧”
140.b47.p: Paper 140 records the day twelve ordinary men were set apart as ambassadors of the kingdom, and it explains at length the life required of them. Jesus did not add rules; he looked at motives, and he asked first about being rather than doing. He gave no solutions to political or economic problems, but he sought to create a new spirit and a new will in men so that they could solve those problems themselves. At the center of all his teaching lies the call to go beyond loving our neighbors as ourselves and to love men as a father loves his children — and the good news that all men are the sons of God.
140.b48.t: The kingdom is not outward show but God within you
The Creator entrusted the work of brotherhood to human hands
The apostles were commissioned to save men, not to judge them
4. You Are the Salt of the Earth
The beatitudes rest on faith and love, not on law
Jesus looks beyond the deed to the motive
The mission is to reveal the Father and lead men to son-consciousness
Jesus taught the inner spiritual life, not reform
Freely you have received, freely give
The good news is that all men are the sons of God
140.b50.box: The ambassadors of the kingdom live not by rules but by the Father’s love, and they proclaim that all men are the sons of God.
141.title: Beginning the Public Work
141.b0.ask: “How is it different when the Father’s will is my law and when it becomes my will — and why does that difference mean being in the kingdom?”
141.b2.p: In Paper 140 the twelve apostles were ordained and consecrated as ambassadors of the kingdom. Now Paper 141 shows them setting out on their public work for the first time. On January 19, A.D. 27, Jesus and the twelve left their Bethsaida headquarters and took the road down the Jordan valley toward Jerusalem.
141.b3.p: Just before they left, Andrew found Jesus sitting in a boat by the shore, weeping. It was not because of any of the apostles; it was because no one of Joseph’s family had come to say good-bye. On the journey that began this way, Jesus passed through Pella, Amathus, Bethany beyond Jordan, and Jericho, teaching his apostles and quietly welcoming John’s disciples.
141.b4.p: In this first public work, then, how did Jesus present God to his apostles? And how did he teach that very different people could be made one?
141.b5.q: “⟦Q 141:2.2⟧When the Father’s will becomes truly your will, then are you in very truth in the kingdom⟦/Q⟧”
141.b8.p: Knowing that Herod would soon take notice of his work, Jesus decided to go south into Judea. They stayed for more than two weeks at the place on the Jordan near Pella where Jesus had been baptized about a year before, and hundreds of people gathered from Galilee, Phoenicia, Syria, the Decapolis, Perea, and Judea. Jesus did no public preaching; Andrew assigned the preachers.
141.b9.p: For John’s disciples, the constant stumbling block was why Jesus did not rescue John from prison. Night after night Andrew taught his fellows how to get along with John’s followers. In the first year of the public ministry more than three quarters of Jesus’ followers had once followed John, and the whole of A.D. 27 was spent quietly taking over John’s work.
141.b10.h: 2. God’s Law and the Father’s Will
141.b11.p: On the night before they left Pella, Jesus declared that the kingdom of heaven is not a rule of the Jews over all peoples but the realization and acknowledgment of God’s rule within the hearts of men. The King of this kingdom is the Father, and we are not only his subjects — we are his sons.
141.b12.t: When the Father’s will is my law
When the Father’s will is my will
In very truth in the kingdom
141.b13.p: No one but James Zebedee grasped the full meaning of this declaration, yet the words sank deep into their hearts and later became the joy of their ministry.
141.b15.p: During nearly three weeks near Amathus the apostles preached twice a day, and Jesus preached only on Sabbath afternoons. When quarrels arose between John’s disciples and the newer disciples, Andrew settled them. Jesus would not step in, saying that “⟦Q 141:3.3⟧a wise parent never takes sides in the petty quarrels of his own children.⟦/Q⟧”
141.b16.t: Personal work and classes for inquirers
141.b17.p: Jesus was a strong and forceful personality. The educated Nicodemus was drawn to him, and so was the Roman centurion at the cross. The book says that the pictures of Jesus have been most unfortunate; had he been the mild, sweet mystic they portray, the temple merchants would hardly have fled before him. Nor did “⟦Q 141:3.8⟧Resist not evil⟦/Q⟧” mean condoning sin; it meant not retaliating against insults to one’s own person, but forgiving.
141.b19.p: Jesus stressed again and again that God is not a bookkeeper who records his children’s sins in order to judge them, but a Father. Never before had so many people thought of God as a Father who loves each individual. When Thomas asked who the God of this kingdom is, Jesus answered that God is your Father, and that the gospel is the faith-recognition of the truth that you are his son.
141.b20.p: Jesus tried to lead the apostles away from the old idea of animal sacrifice, and he taught them to minister to the whole person — body, mind, and spirit united. He divided the afflictions they would meet into three kinds.
141.b21.t: Emotional and mental difficulties and confusion
No longer possible once the Spirit of Truth has been poured out
141.b23.p: When James asked how they might learn to see alike and so live in greater harmony, Jesus was deeply stirred and asked when he had ever taught them to see alike. He did not want harmony bought at the price of free personality and spiritual originality. Spiritual unity comes from knowing that each one is indwelt by the spirit gift of the Father, and it can be enjoyed amid the greatest diversity of thinking, temperament, and conduct.
141.b24.t: Above all, to desire to do the will of the Father in heaven
To find the Father and prove to the universe that we have become like him
141.b25.q: “⟦Q 141:5.1⟧You do not have to see alike or feel alike or even think alike in order spiritually to be alike.⟦/Q⟧”
141.b26.p: Jesus did not want his believers dogmatized and standardized, and he warned again and again against controlling them with creeds or traditions.
141.b28.p: Simon Zelotes tried to win over Teherma, a Persian from Damascus, regarding him as a “fire worshiper,” but failed. Jesus told him not to try to take something out of the heart of one seeking salvation, but only to put something into the hungry soul; lead men into the kingdom, and the living truths of the kingdom will soon drive out error. Simon did so, and Teherma too entered the kingdom.
141.b29.p: That night Jesus said: “⟦Q 141:6.4⟧Do not undertake to show men the beauties of the temple until you have first taken them into the temple.⟦/Q⟧” Introduce men to God first, do not strive with them, and remember that the kingdom is not yours — you are only ambassadors.
141.b31.p: From February 26 they stayed four weeks near Bethany, where John had first proclaimed the kingdom. Jesus spent three days resting in the hills with Peter, James, and John and taught them new truths. The teacher’s one task is to reveal God to the individual as his Father and to lead him to become son-conscious; Jesus left behind no books, no laws, and no organization.
141.b32.p: He stressed two truths above all: salvation by faith alone, and the human liberty that comes from knowing the truth. He came to set a standard of living not just for a few on this earth but for people on all the worlds of the universe, and he was a teacher rather than a preacher.
141.b33.t: What they newly saw in Jesus
He was approachable, yet never swayed by public opinion or praise
He seemed to see the end from the beginning, never excited or discouraged
He was so human, yet without fault, and always unselfish
141.b35.p: While they were at Bethany, Andrew sent the apostles in pairs to Jericho, where John’s believers welcomed the more advanced teaching. Going from house to house to comfort the afflicted, the apostles found that the good news of the kingdom brought great comfort to the sick. The charge to preach the gospel and minister to the afflicted was first fully carried out at Jericho.
141.b36.p: On the way to Jerusalem a delegation from Mesopotamia came to see Jesus, and he changed his plan of staying one day and spent three days with them.
141.b38.p: On the last day of March, Jesus and the twelve climbed the hill road toward Jerusalem. Lazarus of Bethany had made his home ready for their headquarters, and there they rested for five days. For Martha and Mary, welcoming and caring for the Master was a great event.
141.b39.p: On Sunday morning, April 6, Jesus and the twelve entered Jerusalem together for the first time.
141.b41.p: Paper 141 shows how quietly and patiently the first steps of the public work were taken. Jesus welcomed John’s disciples without criticism, took no sides in the apostles’ quarrels, and taught that one should not take anything away from a person of another faith but add to what he has. The God he presented was not a judge who records sins but a Father who loves each person; when we take the Father’s will not as our law but as our own will, we become his free children. And those children, even without thinking alike, can be one in their purpose toward the same Father.
141.b42.t: Section
Key message
1. Leaving Galilee
The first year was a quiet taking over of John’s work
2. God’s Law and the Father’s Will
When the Father’s will becomes our will, we become free children
3. The Sojourn at Amathus
Jesus was not a meek mystic but a strong personality
4. Teaching about the Father
God is not a bookkeeper but a loving Father
5. Spiritual Unity
Not the same thoughts but the same purpose and goal make us one
6. Last Week at Amathus
Do not take away; fill the hungry soul
7. At Bethany Beyond Jordan
Jesus was a teacher who set a standard of living for the whole universe
8. Working in Jericho
Preaching and caring for the sick were first fully carried out
9. Departing for Jerusalem
Jesus and the twelve entered Jerusalem together for the first time
141.b44.box: Children who take the Father’s will as their own are made one in a common purpose, however different they may be.
